title: [2014] 29.639 Billion Yuan: Chinese Cinema Looks Like It's Booming, but Trouble Is Everywhere
body:
## The 2014 film numbers are coming in, and the market everyone was bullish on actually did badly.

Regular article

Mainland box office for 2014 finally settled at 29.639 billion yuan.

It is a slightly awkward record. Growth of 36.15% over the previous year was the highest since 2011, and the prediction that China will become the world's largest film market by 2018 is coming true. Yet a weak New Year season meant 2014 missed the 30 billion mark at the last moment, and people in the industry who had been optimistic are nervous again as they face the new year.

Part of the nervousness comes from Hollywood. *Transformers: Age of Extinction* took 1.97 billion yuan this year, breaking the mainland record that *Avatar* had held for four years. Five of the seven highest-grossing films were Hollywood blockbusters. Imported films accounted for 57% of the 7.87 billion yuan in box office added in 2014, and they took 34 of the year's 52 weekly box-office crowns.

Hollywood studios are trying harder to get into this market. Since Universal Pictures opened its Beijing office, all six major distributors have a command post in China. More and more Hollywood stars are visiting, the studios are hiring local companies to try new kinds of marketing, and they are gradually learning how to sidestep the market's "uncontrollable factors".

So you see *Transformers: Age of Extinction* teaming up with 1905.com, the website run by the Movie Channel. Its head told the media bluntly that Paramount wanted their help to design a story Chinese audiences would like, and to avoid trouble with the censors. Other Hollywood blockbusters must first obtain a public screening permit (the "Dragon Seal" shown at the start of the film) and fix a release date before they can launch large-scale publicity. This film announced its summer release a year in advance, kept announcing Chinese stars joining the cast, and ran big promotional events such as casting calls on the Movie Channel.![Promotional image for Transformers: Age of Extinction](/uploads/image/201501/8599f20a048f.jpg)

That's right: Hollywood's dealmakers are working out the "tricks" of doing business in China, while mainland filmmakers who know those tricks well have hit a bigger problem. They are losing their audience.

Box office for domestic films grew 26.5% in 2014. That is not only below the growth of the market as a whole; it also makes the previous year's 54.3% look glaring by comparison. And domestic films managed even this with protections such as guaranteed release windows and a rule stopping high-grossing imported blockbusters from screening past one month.

The shortage of good content is getting worse. One big-name director after another "fell" at the box office: *Coming Home*, *The Golden Era*, *The Crossing*, *Gone with the Bullets*. These films made little effort to speak to audiences; they felt more like one-man shows the filmmakers staged for themselves. The hits did not satisfy audiences either: *The Monkey King*, *The Break-Up Guru*, *Fleet of Time*. They succeeded in "tricking" people into theaters while using up audiences' trust in Chinese films.

The big old companies are losing their shine, and their rivals jointly handed Huayi Brothers the perfect present for its 20th anniversary. The loudest brand in Chinese film all but vanished from the box-office rankings at the end of 2014. Huayi's top-grossing film last year was *Women Who Flirt*, at 230 million yuan: 20th among domestic films and 41st among all films. Huayi has become a company whose grand plans you can read about in the news, but which cannot give you a good film to enjoy in the cinema.

More and more people entered the industry in 2014, which should have been good news. Resources always flow toward high-return industries and sectors, and an inflow means there is money to be made. But investment funds, video sites, tech companies and film veterans who have spent years in the business alike have shown no convincing grasp of a fast-changing market, whether in making good films or in drawing big box office.

The one consolation is that growth in screens and cinemas will keep paying off for a few more years. Last year China added more than 5,000 screens, bringing the total to 23,600. Strong cinema chains such as Wanda Cinemas are still growing fast. Wanda's box office reached 4.2 billion yuan last year, its lead over the number two chain widened from 1.3 billion to 1.8 billion yuan, and last week it filed again to go public.

Over the past five years, steady growth in cinemas has covered up too many problems and contradictions. Now they are surfacing one by one. We remain optimistic about the future of Chinese film, and amid the chaos the industry is waiting for the next big thing.

This is QDaily's second annual review of the film industry, after "[China's New Film Forces](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/4624)". Starting from last year's box-office numbers, we pick out nine features of the 2014 film market and try to dig into what lies behind the figures.

## 1. Big-name directors can't keep up with the market

The performance of the mainland's big-name directors in 2014 bore out that famous law of nature, "natural selection, survival of the fittest": however strong a species is, if it cannot adapt to changes in its environment (the market), then under fierce competition its decline will come sooner than expected.

A few notorious box-office "disasters" put these "old" directors, born in the 1960s or earlier and made famous in the 1990s, back in the firing line. Ann Hui's *The Golden Era* cost more than 70 million yuan but took only a little over 50 million after opening over National Day. John Woo's *The Crossing* cost 300 million yuan; even with top stars from China, Japan and South Korea and a release in the New Year season, the most lucrative window of the year, *The Crossing* (Part 1) earned just under 200 million. Then there was Jiang Wen's *Gone with the Bullets*, which everyone had awaited for a whole year. It ended flatly amid controversy, and its 510 million yuan so far is far short of the "1 billion at least" people expected.![Still from Gone with the Bullets](/uploads/image/201501/49e4b2a952c4.jpg)

The "old" directors are rapidly losing their pull. In 2013, directors such as Stephen Chow, Feng Xiaogang, Tsui Hark and Peter Chan held key places in the box-office top 10. Among 2014's top 10 domestic films, only two directors, Jiang Wen and Wong Jing, are over 50, while six are under 40. The youngest, Guo Jingming, is just 32.

The young directors' films are far from excellent. Their strengths are a feel for the market, an ability to talk to young audiences, and the capacity to turn out entertainment quickly. But the "old" directors who look down on these films have not won much applause beyond the box office either, compared with their own earlier work.

Yesterday's techniques no longer feel fresh to today's audiences. Resistance to commerce deepens self-absorbed devotion to art; the "meaning" behind a story matters more to these directors than the story itself. Mediocre, strange films get made, and "artistry" becomes the last fig leaf. Don't forget: once you are righteously comparing your film's "quality" with *The Break-Up Guru* and *Fleet of Time*, you have already lost.

These directors' experiments in film art deserve respect, but they must also face a harsh fact: their golden age may really be over.

Unless they shut themselves away in a small dark room and make their own films with no hope of box office, which almost no one can do, they can only adjust and change, work out where the line between creative ambition and the market lies, and do it fast. Today's market and audiences won't give them much room for trial and error.

## 2. National Day and Spring Festival matter more and more

For years, the summer season from June to August and the New Year season from late November to the following January have been the most lucrative and most reliable windows of the year. Last year that changed sharply.

Driven by films such as *Transformers: Age of Extinction*, *The Continent* and *How to Train Your Dragon 2*, the 2014 summer season again did well, with box office up 50% year on year, from 6 billion to 9 billion yuan. Summer kept its high output.

The New Year season was much weaker. With blockbusters such as *The Crossing* (Part 1) and *Gone with the Bullets* doing poorly, the whole season felt "lifeless", and the usual year-end box-office battle between studios fizzled. December box office was 2.57 billion yuan, up 21% year on year, and admissions rose 18%. Both figures trailed the growth in total box office and total admissions for the year, and average attendance per screening actually fell by 0.5 people year on year. The slump was plain.![Chart of New Year season box office](/uploads/image/201501/6a1b5da8b601.jpg)

After the government chopped the public holidays into scattered pieces, the release windows tied to "festivals" opened up new market capacity, most obviously Spring Festival and National Day.

Last year's top-grossing domestic film, *Breakup Buddies*, came out over National Day. The two right behind it, *The Monkey King* and *Dad, Where Are We Going?*, both came out over Spring Festival, as did 2013's box-office champion, *Journey to the West: Conquering the Demons*. Over the past year, Spring Festival and National Day box office rose 84% and 67% year on year, the biggest increases of any window.

So it is no surprise that eight films are set to open together on the first day of this coming lunar new year.

## 3. Ticket prices barely moved, but audiences paid less

Last year, seeing a film in a cinema cost a person 35.67 yuan, up 0.39 yuan from 35.28 in 2013 (with no official data, we divided total box office by total admissions). That is almost no change.

Yet few moviegoers would say tickets got more expensive. On the contrary, for ordinary audiences going to the movies got much cheaper last year. One vivid example: greedy for a bargain, I bought New Year season tickets for 29.9 yuan on Taobao during "Double 11", only to be laughed at by a colleague who later bought tickets on an e-commerce site for 9.9 yuan each.

Because e-commerce platforms such as Taobao, Maoyan, iQiyi and WeChat Movie Tickets are fighting for users, they don't hesitate to sell tickets at rock-bottom prices and then pay the difference to cinemas. The "difference" is the gap between the minimum ticket price the State Administration sets for each city (the least you must pay a cinema at settlement) and the price you actually charge the buyer. It varies by city, usually from ten to several dozen yuan.

Normally, cut-price promotions draw more people into cinemas. But interestingly, neither in December, when promotions were heaviest, nor over the whole year did admissions jump, so it is doubtful whether this approach really helps the box office.

## 4. The top-grossing company of the year

Enlight Pictures took 3.1 billion yuan at the box office in 2014, up nearly 50% from 2.1 billion the year before, making it last year's top-grossing private film company.

Four of its films grossed more than 400 million yuan: the *Dad, Where Are We Going?* movie, *My Old Classmate*, *The Break-Up Guru* and *Fleet of Time*. All were mid-budget films with contemporary, realistic settings, mixing popular elements such as romance and youth, which fits Enlight's usual approach. Its strong distribution arm won Enlight more distribution deals, both for films such as *Dearest* and *Fleet of Time* and for children's films such as *Dad, Where Are We Going?* and *Balala the Fairies*. Distributing so many films is also why Enlight ranked first in overall box office.![Enlight Pictures' 2014 films](/uploads/image/201501/ef15e51913ef.jpg)

The contrast to Enlight is Huayi Brothers, known for its "production strength". The industry's former big brother is having a much harder time. Only in the last two weeks of the year did it get its first film past 200 million yuan, *Women Who Flirt*, which was also its only film of the year to pass that mark. Huayi is now learning from rivals such as Enlight, cutting back on blockbusters and hoping to make more low- and mid-budget films.

The big companies' grip on the industry keeps loosening: 42% of box office came from smaller companies outside the five major private distributors. That gives newer companies such as Ferris Wheel and Gravity Pictures more openings. Last year Ferris Wheel produced *My Old Classmate* and invested in *Breakup Buddies*, with combined box office above 1.5 billion yuan; Gravity invested in *Black & White: The Dawn of Justice* and *Fleet of Time*, and those two films alone grossed nearly 800 million yuan.

## 5. Which films earned the best returns

Of the 241 domestic films released in 2014, fewer than 20% actually made money. We sorted films by production cost and found some with relatively high returns in each range. (Marketing costs vary widely from project to project and are hard to tally, running from several million to tens of millions of yuan.)

Under 10 million yuan: Films in this range rarely get noticed by mainstream audiences and usually target a niche, horror being the classic case. In 2014 a film called *Pen Fairy Horror 3* took more than 50 million yuan on a production cost of 5 million, a profit of more than 200% for its investors and a textbook high-return project. Of course, it was also sued for "parasitic marketing" off the better-known *Pen Fairy 3*, but in the end paid only 500,000 yuan in damages.

20 million yuan: *My Old Classmate* had the highest return in this range, grossing 456 million yuan on a production cost of 20 million. Even counting 20 million in marketing, its return reached 400%. Another money-maker in this range was *Black Coal, Thin Ice*. After winning the Golden Bear for Best Film at the Berlin International Film Festival, it grossed more than 100 million yuan at home and sold rights to 20 countries, so its overall return was handsome.![Still from Black Coal, Thin Ice](/uploads/image/201501/d6d17aab6698.jpg)

50 million yuan: Last year this range produced several hits: *Fleet of Time*, *The Continent* and *The Break-Up Guru*. All three have contemporary, realistic settings combined with one or more of comedy, youth and romance. They took 584 million, 630 million and 666 million yuan respectively, ranking fourth to sixth among domestic films.

80 million yuan: *Breakup Buddies* grossed 1.169 billion yuan, making it last year's top domestic film. Ning Hao + Huang Bo + Xu Zheng + comedy is [the surest winning formula](http://qdaily.com/display/articles/2640) in this market.

Over 100 million yuan: *The Taking of Tiger Mountain* cost between 100 million and 150 million yuan to make. As of January 11, 2015 it had grossed 794 million yuan, securing a place among the year's top three domestic films and leaving its investors grinning.

## 6. Blockbusters are a bad investment

First, some figures for last year's big Chinese-language films: *The Monkey King*, 300 million yuan invested, 1.046 billion box office; *The Crossing*, 300 million invested, 195 million for Part 1; *Gone with the Bullets*, 300 million invested, 511 million box office; *Rise of the Legend*, 130 million invested, 182 million box office.

Box office is split between cinemas and investors. For investors, every 1 yuan put in usually has to generate 3 yuan at the box office just to break even. Keep that in mind and look at the figures again, and you will see why these films' investors were in no mood to celebrate.

Star fees, visual effects and big set pieces are where blockbusters "eat money", and that money buys less and less. The market has changed, and audiences no longer flock to cinemas just for big stars; *The Crossing* is the best example. Next, years of Hollywood blockbusters have raised the bar for effects. Remember how savagely *The Monkey King*, which boasted more than 2,300 effects shots, was panned? And audiences grew tired of costume dramas and spectacle five years ago.![Still from The Monkey King](/uploads/image/201501/65e9f3f195d6.jpg)

Huge budgets also limit release dates. Under pressure to earn back their costs, blockbusters usually have to open in the peak windows (Spring Festival, summer, National Day and the New Year season), which are already crammed and fought over by every studio. That leaves very little room for mistakes or adjustment: start badly, and the next blockbuster in line is likely to knock you out before you can respond, and all your effort goes to waste.

Films closer to audiences' everyday lives, which put in a moderate budget in exchange for a predictable return, are more likely to succeed in this market. Six of 2014's top 10 domestic films cost no more than 50 million yuan to make. Clearly, that range is the safer bet.

## 7. Hollywood keeps panning for gold in China

Last year 33 imported Hollywood revenue-sharing films together took 11.2 billion yuan in the mainland, up 60% from the previous year and 37.8% of total box office. *Transformers: Age of Extinction* alone took 1.97 billion yuan in China, Hollywood's signature event in the Chinese market last year.

Of the 7.87 billion yuan in new mainland box office in 2014, imported films took 4.482 billion, or 56.95%. In other words, imported films reaped more of the gains from market growth. In the 700 million to 1 billion yuan range, imported films went from one in 2013 to four: *Interstellar*, *X-Men: Days of Future Past*, *Dawn of the Planet of the Apes* and *Captain America: The Winter Soldier*. Not a single domestic film landed in that range in 2014. (In 2013 there were two.)

But the Hollywood blockbusters that sell in China are also looking more and more alike, and many interesting films from independent studios are still kept out of the country for reasons we all know.

Once we tire of Hollywood blockbusters, that opens up more opportunity and room for domestic films, so the claim that Hollywood will crush Chinese films completely in 2015-2016 looks too simplistic.

## 8. The 70s, 80s and 90s generations don't watch what they're supposed to

Every film wants to attract every audience in the market, but marketing often starts by choosing one core age group and spreading out from there. This is considered the more effective approach.

So many films give themselves an age label. *Fleet of Time* and *My Old Classmate* both sold themselves on "the youth of the post-80s generation", while *Tiny Times* was clearly made for the post-90s. Some films, such as *Gone with the Bullets* and *The Taking of Tiger Mountain*, sound a bit dated and might be expected to draw post-70s "aunties and uncles".![Chart of film audiences by age group](/uploads/image/201501/0e6f55b3e866.jpg)

In practice it doesn't work that way. According to a survey by Maoyan Movies, *Fleet of Time* and *My Old Classmate*, sold on "post-80s youth", were the post-90s generation's favorite films. The post-80s also like films set further back in time, such as *Gone with the Bullets* and *The Taking of Tiger Mountain*. And the post-70s, besides watching *Coming Home*, also go to *How to Train Your Dragon 2* and *Dad, Where Are We Going?*, mostly as chaperones.

Film companies are not unaware of this mismatch; sometimes they are just playing dumb. *Fleet of Time*, for instance, though sold on "post-80s youth", toured university campuses, where the post-90s gather, and instead of buying big ad campaigns in subways and office towers, where post-80s office workers are concentrated, it generated buzz online. And after *The Taking of Tiger Mountain* opened, plenty of post-80s took their parents and grandparents to see it.

## 9. Audiences in different cities really do watch films differently

Tastes also differ by region. *Breakup Buddies* drew the most admissions in all three of the country's biggest box-office markets, Beijing, Shanghai and Guangdong, but the runners-up differed: *Gone with the Bullets* in Beijing, *The Continent* in Shanghai, and in Guangdong *The Monkey King*, which features several Hong Kong actors.

According to Maoyan Movies' moviegoing report, Beijing has the highest share of people going to early screenings, while Shenzhen loves midnight shows; Shanghai audiences are most likely to pick their own seats; and Changsha has the most people going to the movies alone, earning it the title of loneliest city.
